title: The great Alpha debate
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Christodoulou gives a balanced assessment of Alpha School, the US network where students learn academic content on apps for two hours a day. She likes its use of the science-of-learning based Math Academy, its hiring of talented educators and the principle that a well funded science-of-learning programme would be valuable. She dislikes the gap between thoughtful staff and marketing and boot camp activities she calls Equations Cookbook-style ed tech, and she doubts that content can be unbundled from human experts, especially for young children. She rejects the scaling argument for tech, noting that England's phonics reforms raised check passes from 58 percent in 2012 to 89 percent by 2026 with little technology. She remains pro-experiment and sets testable tests for Alpha, such as an AI maths tutor matching the Google and Eedi work, or 90 percent of over 100,000 pupils passing a phonics check at age seven. She also questions what the claim of learning twice as fast actually means.
points: Be pro-experiment without assuming each experiment works: judge Alpha by clear, testable hypotheses.
Screens suit retrieval practice better than deep reading, and age and novice status limit what children can learn from apps.
It is hard to separate content from the human expert who embodies it, especially for young children.
Technology scales only when it can operate across whole systems, and England's phonics reforms show human-led teaching can scale too.
AI is most promising for screen-free learning, for example handwriting recognition, speech-to-text and spoken practice.
quotes: Historically, so much public and private money in education has been wasted on ideas with very little evidence behind them. For a long time I’ve thought it would be brilliant if either a company or a country put a lot of financial and intellectual resources into building an education programme based on the science of learning
I think screens lend themselves well to rapid retrieval practice, but less well to deep reading. I think that 25-year-olds can learn from screens in ways that eight-year-olds can’t.
I don’t think it is that easy to unbundle the content of learning from its physical manifestation in human experts, particularly when it comes to teaching young children and novices.
You can be in favour of school experiments, as I am, without thinking that every single individual experiment is going to succeed.

Similarly, it’s not contradictory to say that AI is going to be a transformative learning technology, but also that if we want to protect deep learning and thinking, we need time and space in the school curriculum where students read actual books and write their thoughts down about them on paper.

the best human teachers may well be better than an app – but there aren’t very many of them and it’s impossible to create more. The app only has to be better than the median human teacher to be better for most students.
From 2012 to 2019, the percentage passing that check went from 58% to 82%. By 2026, the percentage passing by the end of year 2 was 89%.
I’d like to see an Alpha app or group of schools get 90% of 100k + students to pass some kind of phonics screening check at age 7.
